intro: Searching for the best financial planners near you usually means you want someone local who can look at your whole financial life, not just sell you a product. You may be comparing several people and wondering how to tell them apart. We can introduce you to a suitable UK financial adviser, who will quote you directly, so you can compare and decide for yourself.
need_heading: What people searching for this usually need
need_lead: Most people typing this are looking for someone nearby who can connect the different parts of their finances into one plan.
needs: You have savings, a pension and perhaps a mortgage, and you want someone to look at how they fit together rather than treat each in isolation.
You are approaching retirement and want to understand whether your pension and investments will support the life you hope for.
You have had a life change such as a redundancy, an inheritance or a divorce, and you want help working out what to do next.
You want to know whether your current arrangements are tax-efficient and sensibly protected for your family.
You would prefer to sit down with someone local, or at least speak to an adviser who knows your area and can meet you face to face.
context_heading: Judging who is best for you
context: Nobody can tell you objectively who the best financial planner is, because it depends on your circumstances and what you want from the relationship. What you can do is check that the adviser or firm is authorised, or is an appointed representative of an authorised firm, on the Financial Conduct Authority register, and ask whether their advice is independent or restricted.

Independent advice means the adviser considers the whole market, while restricted advice is limited to certain products or providers, and they must tell you which applies and how they charge. Advanced qualifications such as Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute or the Personal Finance Society, or the CFP certification, can help you weigh up expertise. If something goes wrong you can complain to the firm, then to the Financial Ombudsman Service, and the Financial Services Compensation Scheme may protect you if an authorised firm fails.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe what prompted you to look for a financial planner now, such as a retirement date or a recent change in your circumstances.
Say roughly what you want planned, whether that is pensions, investments, tax, protection or a combination.
Mention whether you already have savings, pensions or investments that need going over, without sharing account numbers.
Explain whether you would like to meet an adviser locally or are happy to work remotely.
Tell us whether you have worked with a financial adviser before and what you did or did not find helpful.
Note any preferences that matter to you, such as independent rather than restricted advice, or a particular specialism.
questions: Are you authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, or an appointed representative of an authorised firm?
Is your advice independent or restricted, and what does that mean for the products you can recommend?
How do you charge for your work, and what will I pay at each stage?
How will you build a plan around my goals, and will you use a cash-flow model to show how it might work?
How often will we go over the plan, and what happens if my circumstances change?
What qualifications do you hold, and do you have a specialism that suits my situation?

faqs.q: How do I check a financial planner is properly authorised?
faqs.a: Look up the adviser or firm on the Financial Conduct Authority register, which shows whether they are authorised or an appointed representative of an authorised firm. This is the most reliable way to confirm they are permitted to give financial advice in the UK.

faqs.q: What is the difference between independent and restricted advice?
faqs.a: Independent advisers consider the whole market, while restricted advisers are limited to certain products or providers. Advisers must tell you which they offer and how they charge, so you can decide what suits you.

faqs.q: Will a financial planner look at my whole situation?
faqs.a: Good financial planning takes a whole-life view, linking your goals with investments, pensions, tax and protection rather than focusing on a single product. Cash-flow models are often used to show how decisions today might affect your future.

faqs.q: What can I do if I am unhappy with the advice?
faqs.a: You can complain to the firm first, and if that does not resolve matters you can take your complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service. The Financial Services Compensation Scheme may also protect you if an authorised firm fails.

extra_heading: Comparing several planners without a league table
extra: Because you are likely weighing up a few names at once, it helps to compare them on the same points rather than on impressions alone. Ask each one the same questions about authorisation, whether their advice is independent or restricted, and how they charge, then set the answers side by side. That way you are judging like for like, and the differences that matter to you become clearer.

The word best also depends on fit. A planner used to working with people building up savings may not suit someone sorting out retirement income, so ask what kind of clients they usually help and whether your situation is familiar to them. A local planner can be easier to meet face to face, but being nearby says nothing about how well they will understand your goals, so let the conversation decide.

Expect the first meeting to be a two-way conversation rather than a sales pitch. A planner is likely to ask about your goals, your pensions, savings, tax and protection arrangements, and what you want the money to do over time, and you should come away knowing whether their advice is independent or restricted and how they charge. If you feel rushed or the answers stay vague, that is useful information when you are comparing.

extra_faqs.q: Is a financial planner the same as a financial adviser?
extra_faqs.a: The terms are often used interchangeably in the UK, and both describe someone who can give regulated financial advice. Financial planning tends to emphasise a whole-life view, linking your goals with investments, pensions, tax and protection, rather than focusing on a single product.

extra_faqs.q: Should I choose someone local even if I mostly deal with them remotely?
extra_faqs.a: Meeting locally can make the first conversation easier, but what matters most is that the adviser is authorised and that you are comfortable with how they work and charge. Many people are happy to work remotely once they have met in person or spoken at length.

extra_faqs.q: How many planners should I speak to before deciding?
extra_faqs.a: There is no set number, but speaking to more than one lets you compare how they explain things and what they charge. Give yourself enough time to weigh up the answers rather than deciding on the first conversation alone.
